transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-03-02 16:00 PST
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (VP Eng - StrataGuard), Owen Park (SRE), Hannah Liu (CTO), Carlos Mendez (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Quick intake to understand StrataGuard's plans for dedicated GPU reservations, isolation needs for models that touch PII, and how to handle bursty traffic from nightly analytics jobs and daytime API spikes.

Topics (auto): reserved sizing, isolation topology, prewarm/hotpool, fallback routing, compliance questions (KMS, audit logs).

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving time. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Priya Desai: Hi Priya here, VP Eng at StrataGuard. Owen and Carlos are with me.
[00:11] Owen Park: Owen Park, SRE.
[00:13] Carlos Mendez: Carlos, ML.
[00:15] Hannah Liu: Hannah, CTO, hopping in for the first 20.
[00:18] Liam O'Connor: Liam O'Connor, SE at Redwood.
[00:21] Maya Chen: Cool, objective for today is to understand your capacity shape and isolation requirements so we can propose reserved GPU options. We'll talk burst strategies and what happens when the dedicated pool is saturated.
[00:35] Priya: Yeah, high level — we run a mix of low-latency chat endpoints for customers (SLA 95th <= 250ms) and heavier nightly batch rerank/embedding jobs; the chat traffic peaks in US-East daytime and we have periodic bursts when clients batch-run requests. We want predictable cost and isolation for certain models that handle PII.
[01:02] Liam: Got it. Are you planning to move all inference to dedicated, or hybrid (hosted + dedicated)?
[01:08] Priya: Likely hybrid. Sensitive models on dedicated private VPC, everything else we might keep on hosted to save cost. But we need headroom for bursts that sometimes double traffic for short windows.
[01:20] Maya: Ok so two requirements: strict isolation for PII models (likely private dedicated) and burst headroom. Can you give us numbers — baseline QPS, peak QPS, and average sequence length?
[01:33] Carlos: Baseline for chat endpoints is about 80 QPS across all customers, peak up to 180 QPS in bursts. Average seq length 120 tokens, but some analytical jobs are 2k tokens. The nightly jobs are throughput heavy but latency tolerant.
[01:48] Owen: Also note our SREs will not accept noisy neighbor effects; we need predictable tail latencies during peak, and we prefer node-level tenancy for strict compliance.
[01:58] Liam: When you say node-level tenancy do you mean physical isolation (dedicated nodes exclusively for your org) or strict tenant fencing with logical isolation?
[02:06] Priya: Prefer physical dedicated nodes if feasible — we have audit/regulatory needs and an internal control that checks for co-tenancy.
[02:14] Maya: We can support private or dedicated with node-level reservation — for Dedicated product you can reserve a set of GPU nodes with isolation. There's also the dedicated + private control plane option for VPC peering, KMS integration, and audit logs.
[02:28] Hannah: Important — can Redwood's private option integrate with our HSM? We need key custody for model encryption at rest.
[02:36] Liam: Yes, we support KMS/HSM integrations — customer-managed keys are supported in Private deployments; on Dedicated we can also integrate with your KMS depending on the topology. We'll include the HSM flow in the security doc.
[02:48] Priya: Ok good. Now about bursts — what's the typical strategy? We don't want to over-provision months of reserved nodes.
[02:58] Liam: Two common patterns: 1) Reserved + Hotpool: you reserve a base capacity and configure a hotpool for prewarmed instances that can be used quickly (but cost is higher), 2) Reserved + Fallback to Hosted: overflow traffic routes to hosted variants or smaller quantized models. Fallback can be policy driven by route or latency.
[03:18] Carlos: For us, fallback to hosted is tricky for PII models. For non-sensitive models it's ok. For sensitive — we want an overflow path that stays within private/dedicated topology, like warmed standby nodes or partner cloud in same VPC.
[03:32] Liam: Understood. For strict isolation we recommend a two-tier reserved pool: dedicated primary nodes (always isolated), plus a private warm standby pool that your org can consume during bursts. That way overflow stays in your tenancy.
[03:46] Maya: Practically, we can size primary for 100 QPS steady, then have a warm pool sized for additional 100 QPS prewarmed but billed at warm rates. Does that pattern map to your cost model?
[03:58] Priya: Sounds reasonable. What's the billing delta for warm prewarmed nodes vs reserved?
[04:04] Liam: Warm pools are typically billed at a lower reserved baseline + a small warm factor; we’ll send exact figures in the proposal. The tradeoff is cost vs tail latency during very short spikes.
[04:18] Owen: One operational question — node turn up and prewarm times. If we need additional nodes after a sudden spike, how long to become available and deliver low 95th latency?
[04:28] Liam: If you rely on autoscale from cold, provisioning can be multiple minutes. Warm pool prewarmed nodes can be ready sub-30s, depending on model size and KV cache warming. For large context models with big KV states, first-token latency still suffers until cache warms.
[04:43] Carlos: That cache warming — is there an automatic KV cache snapshot restore to warm new nodes faster?
[04:50] Liam: We have prefix-cache and KV snapshot features in the runtime; you can preseed caches for common prompts. But it's workload dependent — snapshots help but don't fully replicate live hot cache. We'll capture best practices in the SE doc.
[05:05] Priya: Regarding model variants — can we pin quantized models to reserved nodes and fall back to fp16 hosted if fidelity required?
[05:12] Maya: Yes, model variants and rollout policies are supported. Many customers run quantized int8 on dedicated for cost, and a higher-precision hosted variant as fallback for quality-sensitive routes. We can set automatic rollbacks if evals drop.
[05:25] Hannah: Security question again — audit logs and request tracing. We need end-to-end request tracing and token-level cost breakdown for chargeback.
[05:34] Liam: Console supports token and route level metrics. Audit logs for Private include full request/response metadata (redaction options), SAML SSO, RBAC, and trace IDs you can ingest in your observability stack.
[05:47] Owen: Do you support VPC peering and private IP routing for traffic to remain within our VPC?
[05:52] Maya: Yes, Private deployment supports VPC peering or dedicated interconnect; for Dedicated we offer private network bridges and customer-managed VPC options. We'll enumerate network topologies in the infra sheet.
[06:06] Priya: Great. Let's talk SLOs — our product owners want 95th <= 250ms for chat. Can Dedicated meet that at peak?
[06:15] Liam: For smaller models and short sequences yes, Dedicated can hit low latency targets. For long sequences or very large models, tail can stretch. We recommend benchmarking with your actual prompts. That's part of the POC plan.
[06:29] Carlos: If we need headroom for 180 QPS peaks on 120-token average, any rough node math?
[06:35] Liam: Rough rule: model throughput per GPU depends on model size and batching. For mid-sized LLM (7-13B) with efficient kernels, a node might handle 40-70 QPS with good batching. So to hit 180 QPS with headroom you'd reserve 3-5 nodes as primary and 2-3 warm nodes. We'll run exact sims.
[06:55] Priya: And for the nightly 2k-token jobs — we'd want those to be routed to separate nodes so they don't steal capacity.
[07:03] Maya: We can set routing policies that direct long-running batch jobs to a separate pool with lower priority and different GPU type. That avoids impacting chat.
[07:12] Owen: What about preemption? If we use shared infra for non-sensitive workloads and you preempt, how predictable is that?
[07:20] Liam: For Shared/Hosted we have preemption policies; for Dedicated reserved nodes, preemption doesn't occur. Shared hotpool could be preemptible depending on the subscription. We'll make sure reserved nodes are non-preemptible for your PII models.
[07:33] Carlos: One more question — how do rate limits and quotas interact with dedicated pools? We want per-route quotas and emergency throttles.
[07:40] Liam: Quotas and per-route throttles can be enforced at the gateway level and mapped to model routes. You can set priority queues; lower priority batch jobs will be queued or shunted to batch pools.
[07:51] Hannah: Ok on governance. On the compliance side, we need SOC2, ISO certs, and a runbook for incident response.
[07:59] Maya: We'll attach SOC2 report extract and a runbook skeleton. Also can provide references for customers with similar controls.
[08:09] Priya: Good. Another practical ask — we will need to test scaling behavior with our own traffic. Can Redwood run a perf test in our VPC or do we need to run it from our end?
[08:20] Liam: We typically do joint benchmarks: Redwood SE spins up the test harness in your VPC (requires temporary access + infra checklist) or you can run our load generator. For Private deployments we can run in your environment. For Dedicated we can coordinate a test using sample data.
[08:35] Carlos: We'll prefer you run the harness in our VPC so we capture real network latencies.
[08:39] Liam: Fine by us; we'll include the infra steps.
[08:43] Maya: Ok let's capture immediate asks — primary nodes with physical isolation, warm standby pool for bursts, routing policy to keep PII in dedicated topology, per-route SLAs, and SOC2/HSM integration.
[08:58] Priya: Yes and we want a cost comparison matrix (all dedicated vs hybrid) and a recommended sizing for the next 12 months with scaling curves.
[09:07] Maya: We'll produce a proposal and sizing workbook. Also want to note edge cases: extremely short spikes under 10s — warm pool can handle better than spin up from cold.
[09:18] Owen: Are there telemetry hooks to export token-level traces to our jaeger/tempo?
[09:23] Liam: We have traceID and sampling integration; exporting to Jaeger is supported via OTLP forwarders. We'll add an example config.
[09:31] Hana(n)h: (crosstalk) — spelling name Hannah sorry —
[09:34] Maya: No worries. Any showstoppers we haven't covered?
[09:37] Priya: Not yet, main blockers are cost and KMS/HSM integration verification. If both check out we can move to POC.
[09:46] Maya: Great. We'll get security docs over and a perf plan. Liam, can you outline the bench plan now?
[09:50] Liam: Sure — step 1: baseline profiling using a 1-hour steady-state run at baseline QPS. Step 2: step-up load tests to simulate bursts (30s-5min windows). Step 3: long-run throughput test for 2k-token jobs to validate batch isolation. We'll collect 95th/99th latencies, GPU util, and KV cache warmup curves. We'll also run a cold start test to measure spin up times.
[10:18] Carlos: We'll provide prompt templates and a 24h sample trace.
[10:22] Priya: Timeline — if we get security docs by end of week and bench plan Monday, can we start POC the week of Mar 16?
[10:30] Maya: Yes that aligns. We'll target POC kickoff then.
[10:33] Priya: Great. Anything else?
[10:36] Owen: Minor — our legal team will need standard DPA and data residency language.
[10:41] Maya: We'll include DPA template and residency options.
[10:44] Hannah: Thanks everyone, leaving now — talk soon.
[10:47] Maya: Thanks Hannah. Thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and proposed dates.
[10:52] (meeting closed)
